excluded.reason: Developer/preview URL override guarded by biometrics: internal build tooling, no product relevance for Verevon users
Crash-reporter hook isolation: reliability implementation trivia, not a safety or governance capability
Ads isolation on free tiers: monetisation policy, not a safety capability Verevon plans to offer

clusters.name: Named permission modes / presets (ask, accept-edits, plan, auto, full access)
clusters.description: One selector that sets how much the agent may do without asking, mapped to a bundle of enforceable settings, chosen per thread/project with an inherited default.

bestInClass.why: Codex (q5) defines the richest typed vocabulary (read-only/auto/granular/guardian/full/custom) with a granular approval config per effect class; Antigravity shows the clean preset-to-settings-bundle mapping with per-project inherit; Claude adds plan and auto modes with admin disable switches.

clusters.mechanism: Enum of modes; each mode resolves to a struct {sandbox_mode, approval_policy per effect class (exec, file write, MCP, network, skill), reviewer=user|auto}. Stored per thread with an org/project default ('inherit'); admin requirements remove disallowed modes from the picker; the server, not the client, resolves the effective bundle at run start.

verevon.gap: Posture is server-resolved per profile (chat=auto with read-only tools, Do/deployed_agent=ask) and the autonomy rung is chosen only on plan approval. There is no user-visible, named mode selector persisted per thread or Space (e.g. Ask every time / Auto-review / Full access), and no org default that admins can restrict. Not verified in the composer (check DashboardComposer for a mode picker).
verevon.strengths: Server-resolved posture that the client can only tighten is better than T3 Code's client-side default of full access.

clusters.benefit: Users of the Do/agent page get one understandable control instead of an invisible profile; enterprises can cap autonomy per org. Fits the authority model because the server still resolves the bundle.
clusters.approach: Add a typed AgentMode enum to mp-contracts (ask, auto_review, workspace_write, full) that maps to the existing posture + autonomy rung; persist on the thread in session-core; expose in the Do composer; Control Plane org setting lists allowed modes; model-gateway clamps to min(org cap, user choice).
dependencies: auto-review classifier (C-t3-11-006) for an auto_review mode
clusters.risks: A full-access mode in a hosted product enlarges blast radius; ship it behind admin opt-in.
clusters.rationale: Table-stakes UX in every agent product; Verevon already has the enforcement pieces so this is mostly contract + UI.

clusters.name: Unsafe-mode friction, elevated-risk labels and safe defaults
clusters.description: Confirmation dialogs that list what full access allows, persistent banners while approvals are skipped, consistent 'elevated risk' labelling, and least-privilege shipped defaults.

bestInClass.why: Codex's full-access confirm lists files, terminal, internet and connected apps plus injection/data-loss risks, with a persistent dismissible banner and admin-disabled options; ChatGPT's single shield label is the cleanest cross-product convention; Claude ships every high-risk capability off by default.

clusters.mechanism: Mode change to a risky rung opens a modal listing capability classes and risks (default Cancel); while active a banner shows (dismissable per session or 30 days); every risky toggle carries one shared 'Elevated risk' badge with a Learn-more link; defaults ship off and require per-account opt-in plus a server gate.

verevon.gap: DangerFullAccess requires a typed justification (>=12 chars) on plan approval, which is real friction, but there is no persistent banner while a run holds the highest rung, no shared elevated-risk label vocabulary across settings, and the rung labels are Norwegian-only.
verevon.strengths: Written justification for escalation is stronger friction than a checkbox.

clusters.benefit: Makes Verevon's escalations legible and consistent as more autonomous features (browser, connectors, schedules) ship.
clusters.approach: Frontend Plane: one ElevatedRiskBadge component and copy catalogue (no/en); run header banner when the run's rung is danger_full_access or approvals are auto; Model Plane emits the effective rung on the run stream so the banner is server-truthful.
clusters.risks: Banner fatigue if overused; reserve for the top rung.
clusters.rationale: Cheap, high-visibility trust signal; common across references.

clusters.name: Strict / Lockdown mode (anti-exfiltration profile)
clusters.description: An opt-in or admin-enforced profile that forces human review of every action and closes outbound exfiltration paths (live browsing, agent mode, image rendering, JS).

bestInClass.why: ChatGPT Lockdown Mode (DOC) is the clearest product framing (browsing restricted to cached content, agent and deep research disabled, role-level); Antigravity Strict Mode (SRC) shows the implementation: options carry disabledInSecureMode and lock messages.

clusters.mechanism: A single boolean profile per user/role that (1) forces approval on every effect, (2) disables tools with open-world egress, (3) disables markdown image rendering and browser JS, (4) greys out conflicting settings with a lock reason. Evaluated server-side as a clamp on the mode bundle.

verevon.gap: No lockdown profile. ZDR clamps persistence, not egress; there is no single switch that disables web/browser/connector egress for high-risk users.

clusters.benefit: Gives security-sensitive orgs a one-click posture against prompt-injection exfiltration; composes naturally with the existing server clamp and ZDR posture.
clusters.approach: Control Plane role/org flag lockdown=true; model-gateway profile resolver clamps the tool catalogue (drop web_fetch, browser, provider writes) and forces ask; SPA disables remote image rendering in markdown.
clusters.risks: Users may see a crippled product; explain clearly.
clusters.rationale: Only 3 sources; valuable for enterprise but not blocking.

clusters.name: Declarative permission rules: action(target) with deny > ask > allow
clusters.description: A rule grammar over typed resources (read_file(path), read_url(domain), command(prefix)) with precedence, scopes (global/project/conversation) and wildcard strictness resolution.

bestInClass.why: Antigravity's action(target) grant store with deny>ask>allow and per-conversation grants is the cleanest model; Claude's strictness lattice (blocked>ask>ask-session>allow) with strictest-wildcard folding and lossy merge of wildcard allows is the most rigorous resolution.

clusters.mechanism: Rule = {action, target-pattern, effect in [deny, ask, ask_session, allow], scope, source}. Resolve: exact match first, else fold the strictest over all matching wildcard patterns; deny from any scope wins; a wildcard 'allow' only survives a merge if both layers specify it. Grants are recorded per conversation for 'allow for this chat'.

verevon.gap: capability-core EvaluatePolicy returns Allow/Ask/Deny per capability with signed evidence, and the hook engine supports allow/deny/ask globs, but there is no user- or admin-authored rule set over typed targets, no ask-session level, and editable 'don't ask again' rules are planned only.
verevon.strengths: Central policy decision point with signed Allow evidence and fail-closed unknown tools.

clusters.benefit: Lets users and admins say 'always allow reading this domain' or 'never send mail outside example.com' without code, cutting approval fatigue safely.
clusters.approach: Extend capability-core policy with a rules table (org, Space, user, thread scopes) keyed by capability id + target pattern; resolve strictest-wins in Go; execution-core passes the target (domain, recipient, path) in EvaluatePolicy; SPA 'Rules' settings page.
clusters.risks: Wildcard allows can silently widen; require strictest-wins and audit every rule change.
clusters.rationale: Underpins editable approvals; Verevon has the PDP already.

clusters.name: Shell command static analysis and layered command approval
clusters.description: Parse shell commands (tree-sitter bash/PowerShell) so allow/deny lists match real executables and redirects; parse failure is treated as possible bypass; hardline floors always apply.

bestInClass.why: Cursor's ordered pipeline (parse -> hard deny -> allowlists -> team blocklist -> delete protection -> readonly -> hooks -> mode) on a tree-sitter AST is the most complete; Hermes adds de-obfuscation and a hardline floor that applies even in yolo.

clusters.mechanism: Parse with tree-sitter-bash into executableCommands, redirects and command substitution; if parsing fails or finds dynamic constructs, force a prompt; match each executable against hard-deny, team blocklist and allowlist; recursive delete and history-rewriting git commands always ask.

verevon.gap: No command-level parsing; risk is a substring match on tool names. code_interpreter and process_* run in bwrap with no network, so the need is lower than for local agents.
verevon.strengths: Hermetic sandbox makes command-level policy less critical.

clusters.benefit: Would matter once process_* or networked sandboxes run user-requested commands against Space files.
clusters.approach: Rust: tree-sitter-bash in execution-core for process_start/sh; reject dynamic constructs in Space-write contexts; show parsed executables on approval cards.
clusters.risks: Parser divergence from the real shell; fail closed on parse errors.
clusters.rationale: Verevon is not an IDE and runs commands only in a hermetic sandbox.

clusters.name: Model-based auto-review of risky actions (approve for me / guardian)
clusters.description: A separate reviewer model classifies each risky step as allow, block or escalate so routine actions run without a card while risky or injected ones stop.

bestInClass.why: Codex Guardian v2 (q5) scores the trajectory asynchronously and switches later actions to gated when risk is high, with thresholds and scope config; Claude's auto mode makes the classifier the default with fallbacks; Antigravity adds specialised vetting tools (data flow, dependency, shell change); Hermes adds a consecutive-denial circuit breaker.

clusters.mechanism: Reviewer gets user messages + proposed tool name/arguments (not tool outputs), a policy prompt, and returns {decision, reason, risk 0..1}. Allow below threshold, escalate to a human above it, deny on clear violation; N consecutive denials pause the run; reviewer failure fails closed to a human card; every verdict is logged.

verevon.gap: Only a coarse substring classifier on tool names decides risk; there is no reviewer model, so Do runs either ask for everything risky or nothing.
verevon.strengths: Durable HITL approvals exist to escalate to.

clusters.benefit: Removes approval fatigue from Do-mode and scheduled agents (the Manus-like vision) while keeping injection-driven actions stopped; fits 'Model proposes' because the reviewer only gates.
clusters.approach: execution-core: a Reviewer step between capability policy and HITL; call inference-core with a small model on a cheap route; inputs limited to user turns + tool call; fail closed to CreateApproval; verdicts written to the run trace and audit outbox; ZDR runs use a ZDR-attested reviewer or force a human.
clusters.risks: Classifier false negatives under injection; keep hard floors and never-auto tools outside the classifier.
clusters.rationale: Present in 7 of 12 sources; the main lever for usable autonomous agents.

clusters.name: Classifier policy engineering: intent-clearing rules, argument provenance, tool-result blindness, forced-card escalations
clusters.description: How the auto-review policy itself is written: block rules name what the user's own message must contain, agent-written arguments prove nothing, the classifier never sees tool outputs, and certain conditions always force a human card.

bestInClass.why: Only Claude does this (q5, SRC): a rule template with must-name and clears-when clauses, explicit tool-result blindness against injection, and forceAsk verdicts (discards work, raises permissions, outranks caller) that override auto mode.

clusters.mechanism: Each soft-deny rule = {name, must_name (what the user explicitly asked), action pattern, clears_when}. Tool descriptions list which arguments are agent-authored. Classifier input excludes tool results. A deterministic pre-pass forces a card when the action raises permissions, deletes unsaved work, or would let a routine exceed its caller.

verevon.gap: No classifier, so no classifier policy. The concept of deterministic forced-card checks partly exists as capability Ask.

clusters.benefit: If Verevon builds auto-review, this is the difference between a toy and a defensible reviewer.
clusters.approach: Author the policy as versioned data in capability-core (rules per capability); execution-core composes the reviewer prompt; deterministic forceAsk checks in Rust run before the reviewer.
clusters.risks: Policy prompts drift from tool semantics; test with red-team fixtures.
clusters.rationale: Unique to Claude but directly reusable with C-t3-11-006.

clusters.name: Denied-action equivalence analysis
clusters.description: After a denial, a separate check decides whether a new action is a rephrasing of the denied one so the agent cannot retry around a refusal.

bestInClass.why: Only source; SRC prompt with precise repeat criteria (same violation against the same target).

clusters.mechanism: Keep a per-run list of denials {rule, resource}; before executing a new risky action, compare target/endpoint/intent against the list; repeats are auto-denied with the original reason.

verevon.gap: No denial memory per run.

clusters.benefit: Stops retry loops after a user says no.
clusters.approach: execution-core: store denials on the run; deterministic same-capability+same-target match first, model check optional.
clusters.risks: Over-blocking legitimate variants.
clusters.rationale: Single source; the deterministic version is cheap.

clusters.name: Information-flow control and data classification
clusters.description: Classification levels on sessions, connectors and tools; data may not flow to a destination below its level without approval; sessions taint upward.

bestInClass.why: Manus (SRC) ships admin-defined levels with per-connector input/output levels, allow_downgrade and approval on downward flow; Antigravity's vet_data_flow maps command arguments to source/destination/intent with secrets taint.

clusters.mechanism: Admin defines ordered levels; each session carries a level that rises when it reads higher-classified data; each connector/tool has a max input level; a write whose session level exceeds the destination's input level requires approval or is blocked; downgrades are explicit and audited.

verevon.gap: Verevon has a consent-to-disclose predicate, a restricted-context write block and privacy tiers for routing, but no admin-defined data classification on threads/connectors with session taint and flow approvals.
verevon.strengths: The restricted-context write block is an existing taint primitive.

clusters.benefit: Enterprise customers can stop confidential Data Plane content leaking into Slack/email through agents; aligns with 'Space access never widens an owner-plane ACL'.
clusters.approach: Data Plane labels documents; Model Plane raises a thread's level on retrieval; capability-core stores connector levels; execution-core checks before provider writes and routes to HITL.
clusters.risks: Taint over-propagation makes threads unusable; offer an explicit reviewed downgrade.
clusters.rationale: Enterprise differentiator; Verevon has primitives.

clusters.name: LLM review of configuration changes for security downgrades
clusters.description: Edits to registry, firewall, SSH or telemetry configs are screened by a model for downgrades.

bestInClass.why: Only source.

clusters.mechanism: A diff of the config file is passed to a prompt that flags registry hijack, HTTPS-to-HTTP and disabled verification.

verevon.gap: Not applicable: Verevon's agent does not edit host configuration.

clusters.benefit: Little.
clusters.approach: Do not build.
clusters.rationale: IDE/local-agent concern; Verevon agents work in hermetic sandboxes.

clusters.name: System-prompt confidentiality with decoy answer
clusters.description: Built-in prompts instruct the model to keep instructions confidential and answer probes with a fixed line.

bestInClass.why: Only source.

clusters.mechanism: A prompt clause plus a fixed decoy answer.

verevon.gap: Not checked; low value.

clusters.benefit: Low; prompt secrecy is not a security boundary.
clusters.approach: Skip; treat prompts as non-secret.
clusters.risks: False sense of security.
clusters.rationale: Not a real control and conflicts with Verevon's transparency goals.

clusters.name: Agent-browser governance: site allow/block lists, per-site consent, JS policy, origin trust
clusters.description: Controls on where and how the agent's browser may act: per-site first-action consent and 'always allow', admin allow/block lists, site categories, JS execution policy, private-network origin pinning, per-tab authorisation.

bestInClass.why: Claude combines per-site consent with prohibited sensitive actions (DOC), an admin default site policy with allow/block lists and localhost carve-out, and DNS address pinning for trusted private origins (SRC q5); Perplexity Comet's per-domain Browser Control / Read Only / No Access is the clearest user model.

clusters.mechanism: Per (org, user) site table: domain -> {control | read_only | no_access, source}; first action on a new domain asks; admin lists override user lists (block wins); sensitive actions (login, purchase, download, permission grant) always ask; private-network origins only when trusted and the resolved IPs match pinned addresses; per-run grant carries the allowed domains.

verevon.gap: No baseline record covers this directly (SRC check done here). The browser-broker grant already carries a canonical AllowedDomains list (max 32) and AllowedActions for sensitive scopes, and execution-core classifies risky browser actions (login, checkout, form post, cross-domain, cookies) into durable approvals. Missing: (1) grants are never minted for chat (BFF sends grant_id 'session:{id}'), so agent browser runs fail closed; (2) no per-site consent memory or user/admin allow/block list UI; (3) no site-category screening.
verevon.strengths: Model proposes, Quarry executes; broker-owned immutable domain policy per grant; risk classes with HITL.

clusters.benefit: The browser agent is central to the Manus/Perplexity-like vision; per-site consent is what makes users trust it.
clusters.approach: Control/Space decision mints a browser-broker grant per run with AllowedDomains derived from the user's site table + admin lists; Model Plane stores the site table (capability-core); SPA consent card 'Allow on example.com: once / always / read-only'; Quarry rejects navigation outside the grant.
clusters.risks: Domain lists are coarse against redirects and embedded frames; Quarry must re-check on every navigation.
clusters.rationale: Agent browser runs cannot start today; this unblocks a headline capability with governance built in.

clusters.name: Per-call sandbox escalation with justification
clusters.description: When the sandbox blocks something, the model asks in the same tool call for the narrowest wider permission with a stated reason, which the user approves.

bestInClass.why: Codex's schema (sandbox_permissions use_default|with_additional_permissions|require_escalated, justification, reusable prefix_rule, additional fs/network) is the most complete; DeepSeek enforces narrowest-wider-mode and a single retry.

clusters.mechanism: Tool schema field sandbox_permissions plus justification; the runtime shows a card with the delta; approval can store a reusable prefix rule; denial is reported back to the model.

verevon.gap: Shipped as an autonomy ladder per call with justification (deepseek-harness design). Missing: reusable prefix rule on approval and additional_permissions granularity (network vs filesystem).
verevon.strengths: Per-call ladder with mandatory justification is in contracts and matches the best references.

clusters.approach: Keep; later add an approved_with_amendment decision so one approval can become a scoped rule.
clusters.rationale: Verevon is at parity here.

clusters.name: Approval request/decision contract with scopes (once, session, always, amend)
clusters.description: A typed, server-initiated approval request carrying the reason and suggested rules, and decisions that carry a permanence class (once, this session, always, with rule amendment); fail closed when no answerer.

bestInClass.why: Codex's bidirectional JSON-RPC (q5) has typed request variants and decisions approved / approved_for_session / approved_with_amendment / denied / abort; Claude's can_use_tool carries reasons, matched rule and permanence and coerces one-click 'always' to session scope; DeepSeek proves the fail-closed seam (no answerer = denied).

clusters.mechanism: Request {kind, tool, args, reason_code, matched_rule, suggestions[]}; Decision {behavior allow|deny, scope once|session|always, updatedInput?, ruleUpdates[]}; 'always' from a card is stored at session scope unless confirmed in settings; a missing or throwing answerer resolves deny; pending approvals survive restarts.

verevon.gap: Approvals are durable rows in session-core with Approve/Reject only; no 'allow for this run/thread' scope, no rule amendment, and 'don't ask again' rules are explicitly not built. After approval only three effect kinds are re-executed and the LLM loop does not resume (runtime gap).
verevon.strengths: Durable, restart-safe approvals with encrypted exact-effect descriptors (T3 Code's in-process approvals go stale on restart).

clusters.benefit: Without scoped decisions every repeated action asks again, which makes Do-mode tiring; with them Verevon matches Codex/Claude while keeping durability.
clusters.approach: Extend orchestration.proto Approval decision with scope and rule_updates; session-core stores session-scoped grants keyed by run/thread + capability + target hash; execution-core consults them before HITL; SPA card adds 'Allow for this run' and 'Always (review in settings)'.
dependencies: LLM loop resume after approval (runtime category)
clusters.risks: 'Always' scope widening; keep it session-scoped by default and audited.
clusters.rationale: Users notice immediately; blocks a usable agent page.

clusters.name: Approval card content: exact command, permission delta, human-readable templates, anti-decoy display
clusters.description: What the approval card shows: the exact effect, the permission delta (network, write paths, escalation), a plain-language sentence per connector tool, recipient fields first with decoy warnings, and execution-time re-check of what the card promised.

bestInClass.why: Claude's anti-decoy card (recipients first, duplicate 'to' spellings flagged, truncation disclosed) and app-written plan fingerprint re-checked at execution are unique and q5; Codex's 55 versioned templates ('Allow GitHub to add a comment to PR #x?') and Manus's permission-delta badges complete it.

clusters.mechanism: Template registry keyed by (connector, tool) with labelled params; card renders recipients/subject first, flags duplicate recipient keys, discloses truncation; app (not model) writes the plan summary with a fingerprint; executor re-verifies the effect matches the approved descriptor.

verevon.gap: No baseline record; SRC from the baseline narrative. Cards show Approve/Reject with tool name/arguments; strings are partly Norwegian-only. Missing: per-tool human-readable templates, recipient-first/anti-decoy rendering, permission-delta badges.
verevon.strengths: Execution re-checks an encrypted exact-effect descriptor and runs a postcondition read-back, equal to Claude's execution-time re-check.

clusters.benefit: Users approve what they understand; reduces social-engineering via injected recipients.
clusters.approach: capability-core holds templates per provider action; execution-core attaches a rendered summary + structured fields to CreateApproval; SPA renders recipients first with decoy warnings.
clusters.risks: Template drift from real arguments; render raw args behind a disclosure.
clusters.rationale: High user-facing value; partly built.

clusters.name: Approvals off-surface: OS/push notifications, remote device, child-session relay
clusters.description: Pending approvals reach the user when they are not looking: OS or push notifications with limited actions, approval from another device only for tools that do not run locally, relay from dispatched child sessions to the parent.

bestInClass.why: Only Claude (SRC): notifications drop the 'Allow' action for high-risk tools so they must be approved on the card; child-session permission relay; remote approval restricted by where the tool executes.

clusters.mechanism: On approval_requested: push a notification {title, tool, session}; include an Approve action only for low-risk classes; deep link to the card; child runs forward requests to the parent thread.

verevon.gap: No baseline record. Check whether Application Plane notifications fire on awaiting_approval for Do and scheduled runs, and whether subagent approvals surface on the parent run.

clusters.benefit: Long agent runs stall silently on approvals today unless the tab is open; notifications fix that.
clusters.approach: Model Plane publishes approval.requested on NATS; Application Plane notification projection delivers in-app/web push; approve action for low-risk only.
clusters.risks: Approving from a notification without context; restrict to low-risk.
clusters.rationale: Single source, but matters for background agents.

clusters.name: Unattended / scheduled run approval policy
clusters.description: What happens when nobody can answer: headless modes default to deny, scheduled runs auto-approve only narrowly stored unexpired rules, some tools are never delegable, unattended prompts are injection-scanned and auto-paused.

bestInClass.why: Claude's shouldAutoApprovePermission (stored rules with expiry, non-delegable browser/computer/skill/memory/schedule tools) is the most precise; Hermes's cron/single-query/unattended modes default to deny with a narrowed toolset and auto-pause on injection hits.

clusters.mechanism: Each schedule stores approvedPermissions [{tool, rule, expiresAt}] captured at creation; at run time a request is auto-approved only if every suggested rule is covered and unexpired and the tool is delegable; otherwise the run pauses with an instructive denial; prompts of unattended jobs are scanned before execution.

verevon.gap: Scheduled effects need Control-signed decisions (strong), but scheduled steps are a single no-tool call today, and there is no per-schedule stored approval set with expiry or non-delegable tool list; unattended identity and guards (D10/D11) are planned.
verevon.strengths: Control-signed per-effect decisions for cron/watch are stricter than any reference.

clusters.benefit: Scheduled and background agents (Manus-style) are core to the vision; they need a defined approval contract before they get tools.
clusters.approach: session-core: schedule.approved_capabilities with expiry captured at creation from an explicit consent card; execution-core: unattended runs consult it and otherwise pause with a durable approval + notification; never-delegable list in mp-contracts.
clusters.risks: Stale consents; enforce expiry and show them in settings.
clusters.rationale: Blocks tool-using scheduled agents.

clusters.name: Never-auto-approvable tools and the self-escalation ratchet
clusters.description: Tools that always need a human card regardless of mode, and a ratchet so the model cannot raise its own permission mode or change settings without a card.

bestInClass.why: Claude (q5) keeps static sets that require approval in every mode and ranks modes so any self-requested increase is card-only; nonce-bound consent for self-management tools.

clusters.mechanism: Static never_auto set in contracts; permission-mode tool compares rank(requested) > rank(current) -> card; consent nonces bind the approved request.

verevon.gap: The client can only tighten the posture and the model has no tool to change its own mode, so the ratchet effectively holds. Missing: an explicit, declared never-auto class that survives a future auto-review or full-access mode (verify capability-core for an equivalent).
verevon.strengths: Server-resolved, tighten-only posture.

clusters.benefit: Becomes essential the moment auto-review or full-access modes exist.
clusters.approach: mp-contracts: RiskClass::NeverAuto on capabilities (payments, external sends to new recipients, memory/skill writes, schedule creation); execution-core forces HITL for them in every mode.
clusters.rationale: Small, prevents a class of regressions.

clusters.name: Filesystem boundaries and folder grants
clusters.description: Agent file access confined to workspace roots, outside reads need approval, folder grants are first-class state, path containment uses realpath and rejects alternate spellings.

bestInClass.why: Claude validates folder grants before the prompt (network drives, UNC, protected host locations) and confines file tools with alternate-spelling rejection; T3 Code shows lexical + realpath containment at every I/O site.

clusters.mechanism: Grant store per session; canonicalise (realpath) and reject UNC/network/protected roots; enforce at every file I/O; reads outside roots ask.

verevon.gap: No baseline record in this category; the baseline narrative shows bwrap + Landlock with ReadOnly/WorkspaceWrite policy and Space-scoped workspace leases. Local folder grants do not apply to a hosted web product.
verevon.strengths: Kernel-enforced confinement on the server rather than path checks in the app.

clusters.approach: Keep. If a desktop/local connector is ever added, adopt Claude's pre-prompt path validation.
clusters.rationale: Verevon has server-side confinement; local folder grants do not fit.

clusters.name: Protection of agent persistence and self-modification points
clusters.description: Even inside a writable area, the agent cannot write its own config, hooks, permission files, interpreter or checkout; auto-executing config is dropped when files cross trust boundaries.

bestInClass.why: Cursor's hard-coded protected-path list (q5) and Claude's protected-subpath deny rules for shell profiles and agent config; Hermes protects its interpreter and checkout.

clusters.mechanism: Deny-write list evaluated before any write; explicit carve-outs where the agent is meant to author (skills folder) go through a separate gate.

verevon.gap: No baseline record. Check whether any Do-mode tool can modify agent skills, instructions or memory configuration outside session-core's governed APIs (reattach_skill exists).

clusters.benefit: Prevents a prompt-injected agent from planting persistent instructions for future runs.
clusters.approach: Keep all persistent agent state behind session-core APIs with their own gates (see C-t3-11-021); sandbox images mount no agent config.
clusters.rationale: Mostly a local-agent concern; Verevon's server design likely covers it.

clusters.name: Memory and skill write governance
clusters.description: Cross-session memory and skill writes are governed: optional user approval with staged entry-pinned writes, injection scans at write and load, write authority limited to the primary agent, read-before-write for autonomous edits, egress redaction to memory providers.

bestInClass.why: Hermes (q5, SRC) is the only source with a full design: staged writes replay only if the pinned entry still exists, the background review fork can only use memory/skill tools with approvals auto-denied, and skill patches require a fresh read.

clusters.mechanism: Memory write -> scan (injection/exfil patterns) -> if write_approval: stage {op, pinned_entry} for review -> apply only if the pinned entry is unchanged; subagents/cron cannot write; memory is re-scanned when loaded into a prompt.

verevon.gap: No baseline record in this category (SRC check here). Dreaming extraction treats content as untrusted: model names closed memory slots, never DB keys; closed scope/kind sets; confidence floor and per-call cap; rows tagged extractor:llm so users can see inferred memories. Missing: optional user approval/staging of memory writes, injection scan of memory text at write and at load, explicit rule that subagents cannot write memory (verify).
verevon.strengths: Closed-slot extraction with provenance tags is a strong, Verevon-specific design.

clusters.benefit: Memory that learns about the user (the Hermes goal) is a prime persistent-injection target; governed writes keep it trustworthy.
clusters.approach: session-core: run scan_injection on every memory value before accept and when building memory_prefetch; optional per-user 'review new memories' queue reusing the approvals table; deny memory writes from subagent and scheduled contexts.
clusters.risks: Review queues nobody reads; default to auto-accept with visible provenance.
clusters.rationale: Memory is a headline differentiator; protecting it is cheap relative to its value.

clusters.name: Prompt-injection defences (untrusted-content labelling, scanning, sanitisation, layered monitoring)
clusters.description: Every untrusted tool/web/MCP result is labelled as data, scanned for injection patterns, stripped of invisible Unicode and forged envelope tags, and monitored by classifiers.

bestInClass.why: Perplexity documents the most layered stack (intent anchoring, BrowseSafe screening classifier, containment, runtime monitoring, red-teaming; DOC); Claude's homoglyph-aware scrubber that neutralises forged host envelope tags is the best concrete code (q5 SRC); Hermes strips invisible Unicode tag characters and reserved _meta from MCP results.

clusters.mechanism: Normalise untrusted text (NFKC, strip U+E0000 tag block and zero-width chars, neutralise lookalike '<' + reserved tag names); wrap in a trust-class envelope; tiered pattern scan (strict for context files/memory, advisory for tool results); semantic classifier on external content; user intent anchoring in the system prompt.

verevon.gap: Trust-class provenance, a fail-closed scan over the full payload before truncation and hash-only security events are shipped. Weaknesses: scan_injection is a lowercase substring match over a marker list with no Unicode/homoglyph normalisation or invisible-character stripping (SRC moderation.rs:183-186); the semantic ContentSafety pass runs in shadow, not enforcing.
verevon.strengths: Trust-class envelope and scan-before-truncation are ahead of DeepSeek/Manus labelling; hash-only security events.

clusters.benefit: Injection is the main risk once browser and connectors run; normalisation closes cheap bypasses.
clusters.approach: model-gateway moderation.rs: add a normaliser (NFKC, tag-block/zero-width strip, confusable folding) before scan_injection; neutralise forged envelope tags in untrusted text; promote semantic_screening from shadow to enforce for ExternalWeb/Browser trust classes after measuring false positives.
clusters.risks: Over-blocking legitimate pages; enforce by trust class.
clusters.rationale: Verevon is already strong; upgrades are incremental but important.

clusters.name: Content moderation, safety banners and policy-error transparency
clusters.description: Input/output moderation with user-facing safety banners, warnings, reports and appeals, and typed policy errors that tell the model and user what happened.

bestInClass.why: Claude shows dismissible safety banners for sensitive topics with resource links and model-fallback explanations; Codex returns typed safety errors (cyber, bio) with a steering hint; Manus has report/appeal flows.

clusters.mechanism: Moderation verdict -> typed event {category, action, user_copy, resources}; the SPA renders a banner; a report button posts to a review queue; refusals are typed and localised.

verevon.gap: A moderation enforcement point exists but input/output enforcement is incomplete and the semantic pass is shadow-only; no safety banners or report flow found in the chat page (not searched exhaustively).
verevon.strengths: A typed, localised refusal catalogue (built for ZDR) is the right pattern to extend to safety refusals.

clusters.benefit: A public chat product needs visible, explainable moderation for trust and compliance (EU AI Act transparency).
clusters.approach: Extend the typed refusal catalogue with safety categories; model-gateway emits safety_notice events; SPA banner + report action into Application Plane.
clusters.risks: Over-moderation hurts B2B usefulness.
clusters.rationale: Common; partly built.

clusters.name: Computer-use safety (per-app grants, app tiers, input guardrails, overlay and hard stop)
clusters.description: Guardrails for an agent controlling a desktop: per-app grants with TTL, view-only tiers for browsers/trading apps, blocked OS shortcuts, secure-field blocks, a visible overlay and a hard-stop hotkey.

bestInClass.why: Claude's app tiering (browsers/trading read-only, terminals click-only) and protected-field blocks are q5 unique; Manus's always-visible overlay with Shift+Esc stop is the best UX.

clusters.mechanism: Classify target app -> access tier; per-app grant with expiry; key-chord filter; refuse typing into password fields; overlay while controlling; global stop.

verevon.gap: OS-level computer use is parked by the owner; no Model Plane path.

clusters.benefit: Only relevant if computer use is revived.
clusters.approach: Skip now; if revived, model these as Quarry-side executor rules.
clusters.rationale: Parked by the owner; hosted browser covers the near-term need.

clusters.name: Model-blind credentials and login handling for the agent browser
clusters.description: The agent can log in or fill secrets without seeing them: secret references substituted by the executor with origin binding, vault autofill, sensitive-field denial, takeover for logins, selective import of browser sessions.

bestInClass.why: Manus (q5 SRC): the model types {{secret:name.field}}, the operator substitutes only when the live frame origin matches allowed hosts, mixed text gets no sensitive-input authority, and password/payment fields reject plain-text input; Hermes's vault fill re-asserts origin inside the injected script and registers exact bytes for redaction.

clusters.mechanism: Vault items bound to origins; model sees handles only; executor validates live document origin (deny opaque/sandboxed frames), fills the field, registers the value with the redaction boundary; plain typing into password fields is refused; otherwise hand off to human takeover.

verevon.gap: No baseline record. Browser risk classes route login and cookie use to HITL, and Quarry's manual browser supports human takeover (live-proven per the parity audit, DOC). Missing: a vault of origin-bound secret references substituted by Quarry so the model never sees credentials.
verevon.strengths: Model proposes, Quarry executes is exactly the split needed for executor-side substitution.

clusters.benefit: Lets agents work on sites behind login (Manus's core use case) without leaking credentials into model context or ZDR-violating logs.
clusters.approach: Control Plane or integration-corev2 holds an encrypted per-user vault; browser-broker grant lists allowed secret handles + origins; Quarry substitutes at execution; Model Plane only passes handles; redaction registry in sandbox/Quarry output.
clusters.risks: Vault is a high-value target; origin binding must fail closed.
clusters.rationale: 5 sources; key to useful browser agents.

clusters.name: Agent payments with one-time cards and per-purchase approval
clusters.description: Agents buy on the user's behalf through a linked wallet with one-time virtual cards; each order shows merchant and line items for approval; card numbers never reach the model.

bestInClass.why: Manus is the only source (SRC); Stripe Link one-time cards exported to an owner-only directory and referenced by token.

clusters.mechanism: Wallet link (Stripe Link); per purchase: approval card with merchant, items, total; mint a one-time card; executor fills standard autocomplete fields from a temporary reference.

verevon.gap: No payment capability (book_shipment books shipments through a provider API, not card payments).

clusters.benefit: Would enable end-to-end errands; large compliance surface.
clusters.approach: Defer; if built, keep it in integration-corev2 with step-up verification (C-t3-11-049).
clusters.risks: Fraud and liability.
clusters.rationale: Unique to Manus; not core for a B2B launch.

clusters.name: Credential storage and secret references
clusters.description: API keys and tokens are stored in OS keystores or encrypted stores, referenced by name in config, write-only in the UI, resolved in a fail-closed per-profile scope, optionally sourced from external secret managers.

bestInClass.why: Hermes's context-scoped secret resolution that raises instead of falling through to the environment (q5) is the best multi-tenant pattern; DeepSeek shows write-only keys with source disclosure; Cursor's team/personal keyrings for cloud agents are closest to Verevon's hosted model.

clusters.mechanism: Secrets live in a per-tenant encrypted store; config holds references; resolution uses a request-scoped context and fails if unscoped; the UI shows source (env/vault) but never the value; cloud-agent secrets are granted per agent and injected only at execution.

verevon.gap: No baseline record. Approval continuation descriptors are encrypted; connector tokens live server-side in integration-corev2 (INF from the baseline narrative). Check whether users can store secrets for agents/sandboxes and how integration-corev2 stores OAuth tokens.

clusters.benefit: Needed for user-supplied API keys in sandboxes and BYO-model connections (the planned own-connection ZDR waiver).
clusters.approach: Control Plane (or integration-corev2) secret store with per-org KMS keys; references in run configs; execution-core resolves into sandbox env only for the lease lifetime.
clusters.rationale: Most reference items are desktop keychain concerns.

clusters.name: Secret and PII redaction in outputs and logs
clusters.description: Sensitive strings are redacted from tool outputs, logs and telemetry; best designs make leaks impossible by type (RedactedString) or by exact-value registration.

bestInClass.why: Cursor's RedactedString type that refuses implicit serialisation (q5) prevents accidental leaks by construction; Hermes registers exact vault values for scrubbing plus regex redaction.

clusters.mechanism: Wrapper type with Debug/Display/Serialize returning '[redacted]'; explicit expose() at the boundary; exact-value registry for secrets filled at runtime; regex pass on tool results.

verevon.gap: Regex scrubbing of step payloads and sandbox output, and opt-in PII redaction before provider calls are shipped. Possible improvement: a Rust newtype for secrets (e.g. secrecy::SecretString) used across services, and exact-value registration once a vault exists.
verevon.strengths: Scrubbing on both Rust and Go sides plus opt-in PII redaction before inference.

clusters.approach: Keep; adopt a secret newtype in mp-contracts.
clusters.rationale: At parity or ahead.

clusters.name: Child-process environment and proxy hygiene
clusters.description: Subprocesses get a filtered environment (provider keys removed, explicit passthrough); project files cannot redirect proxies; shells are not persisted with brokered credentials.

bestInClass.why: Hermes uses one env builder with a provider-key blocklist for every child type; DeepSeek refuses project .env proxy variables.

clusters.mechanism: Build child env from an allowlist; drop *_API_KEY and tokens; proxy settings only from the trusted launcher.

verevon.gap: No baseline record. Check that bwrap invocations clear the environment (--clearenv) and pass only an allowlist into code_interpreter/process_* children.

clusters.benefit: Defence in depth for the sandbox.
clusters.approach: Verify; if missing, add --clearenv + allowlist in sandbox.rs.
clusters.rationale: Likely already covered by the hermetic design; verify.

clusters.name: Credential isolation from sandboxes and credential-injecting egress proxies
clusters.description: Sandboxes never hold real credentials: connector auth stays server-side, and sandboxed CLIs get fine-grained resource grants enforced by an egress proxy that swaps opaque tokens for real ones.

bestInClass.why: Antigravity's permissioned GitHub grants (binary.action(resource) with org/repo mandatory) enforced at a TLS-intercepting proxy (q5) is the most precise; Hermes's iron-proxy shows the token-swap mechanics.

clusters.mechanism: Sandbox gets HTTPS_PROXY + CA; proxy maps opaque token -> real credential per host; requests checked against granted resource scopes; blocked requests return a message to the model.

verevon.gap: No baseline record (SRC check here). Provider actions run server-side through integration-corev2, so connector credentials never enter the sandbox (INF from the code layout); MpNetworkPolicy::AllowDomains relies on an egress proxy and the executor must fail closed without one. No credential-injecting proxy for sandboxed tools.
verevon.strengths: Server-side provider actions keep tokens out of model and sandbox.

clusters.benefit: Needed only when sandboxed code must call authenticated APIs (e.g. git push from a Space workspace).
clusters.approach: Extend the egress proxy behind AllowDomains with per-lease opaque tokens resolved by sandbox-manager; scope grants per resource.
clusters.risks: TLS interception complexity.
clusters.rationale: Verevon's architecture already avoids the main risk.

clusters.name: Sandbox network egress policy tiers
clusters.description: Admin- and user-selectable network posture for agent sandboxes and browser sessions: off / package managers only / allowlisted domains / all, as policy sets with globs and CIDRs.

bestInClass.why: Claude.ai's four tiers with plan-dependent defaults applied to new sessions (DOC q5) is the clearest product; Manus (SRC) shows admin policy sets in allow/block mode with glob + CIDR applied to sandbox and browser; Cursor lets admins lock local, MCP and cloud egress separately.

clusters.mechanism: Policy set {mode allowlist|blocklist, patterns[], cidrs[]} per org; tier enum on the sandbox lease; enforced by a proxy (domains) plus a net namespace (off); changes apply to new leases; the model is told the current tier.

verevon.gap: No baseline record (SRC check here). MpNetworkPolicy has Disabled and AllowDomains variants, and the code requires fail-closed behaviour without an egress proxy; code_interpreter ships with no network. Not found: an org/user-facing tier setting, a package-manager tier, or a deployed egress proxy (verify).
verevon.strengths: Fail-closed network policy type already in contracts.

clusters.benefit: Data analysis that needs pip/npm or public APIs is a common user request; tiers make it safe.
clusters.approach: capability-core org setting network_tier; sandbox-manager stamps it on the lease; execution-core maps it to MpNetworkPolicy; deploy an egress proxy with a curated package-registry allowlist.
clusters.risks: Package registries are an exfiltration and supply-chain channel; log all egress.
clusters.rationale: Common in references; the contract is half built.

clusters.name: SSRF guard with DNS-rebinding closure
clusters.description: Server-owned HTTP paths refuse private, internal and metadata addresses, re-checking at connect time and on every redirect.

bestInClass.why: Only reference source; checks at TCP connect and per redirect.

clusters.mechanism: Resolve -> check IP against deny CIDRs -> pin the address for the connection -> re-validate each redirect.

verevon.gap: Shipped for webhooks/remote_trigger, MCP OAuth discovery and MCP DNS revalidation. Verify the same guard covers web_fetch and Quarry fetches.
verevon.strengths: At parity with the best reference.

clusters.approach: Keep; extend to every server-side fetch path.
clusters.rationale: Verevon equal.

clusters.name: OS-level sandbox for agent commands and named permission profiles
clusters.description: Commands run under kernel isolation (bwrap/Landlock/seccomp, Seatbelt, restricted Windows tokens, containers) with named profiles for filesystem roots, deny-read paths and network.

bestInClass.why: Manus's Windows safe mode (dedicated account, restricted token, per-root capability SIDs, persistent WFP block; q5) is the deepest local implementation; Codex's named permission profiles with special paths, globs and deny-read tables are the best policy vocabulary.

clusters.mechanism: Profile {writable_roots, deny_read, network} -> backend argv (bwrap --ro-bind / Landlock rules / seccomp filter); probe at boot and refuse to run when the backend is unavailable.

verevon.gap: No baseline record in this category; the baseline narrative shows bwrap + Landlock/seccomp with ReadOnly/WorkspaceWrite and a network policy, probed at boot. Gap: isolation is per call inside the execution-core container, with no VM/container per session (deferred SandboxBackend seam).
verevon.strengths: Kernel-enforced, boot-probed sandbox on the server.

clusters.approach: Keep; build the SandboxBackend seam before adopting VM sandboxes (runtime category).
clusters.rationale: Verevon equal for its hosted model.

clusters.name: Sandbox enforcement and denial transparency
clusters.description: Each sandbox result states whether enforcement was full or partial, distinguishes a policy denial from a runner failure with a visible marker, and records structured violations that can become policy amendments.

bestInClass.why: DeepSeek (SRC) reports enforcement as a fact per call and matches denial signatures (EROFS, EACCES, EPERM) only after runner-failure rules, fixing a misclassification it documented in a postmortem; Codex records violations centrally and proposes amendments.

clusters.mechanism: Backend returns {enforcement full|partial, denialSignatures, runnerFailureRules}; result carries sandbox {mode, denied}; a denial marker is appended for the model; violations stored with what/where/why and an optional suggested rule.

verevon.gap: No baseline record. Check whether code_interpreter/process results tell the model and user that a failure was a sandbox denial (e.g. network disabled) rather than a code error, and whether partial Landlock ABI support is reported.

clusters.benefit: Matches Verevon's honesty/transparency contracts and the DeepSeek reference goal; prevents the model from 'fixing' code that failed due to policy.
clusters.approach: execution-core: classify bwrap/Landlock denials, attach sandbox{mode, denied, enforcement} to tool results and the trace; render a 'blocked by sandbox' chip in the SPA.
clusters.rationale: Cheap; strong fit with Verevon's transparency principle.

clusters.name: Admin agent-policy registry and organisation setting locks
clusters.description: A typed registry of admin-controllable agent behaviour (allowed modes, browser/MCP/connector toggles, egress, retention, telemetry) with per-key fail-closed values, tighten-only remote config and visible lock states.

bestInClass.why: Claude's schema-as-source-of-truth registry (183 keys) with an explicit fail-closed value per key, restrictions-before-grants and tighten-only unverified config (all q5 SRC) is unmatched; Codex's requirements allow-lists and ChatGPT's Requirements-vs-Defaults per environment are the best admin UX framing.

clusters.mechanism: Each key = {schema, default, failClosedValue, scopes, lockable, restrictiveDirection}; resolution merges org requirement (cannot be overridden) over org default over user choice using most-restrictive-wins; unreadable or invalid -> failClosedValue; the UI shows 'managed by your organisation'.

verevon.gap: Control Plane admin covers members, SSO, org security, trust and quotas, and capability-core has rollout/scopes per capability. Missing: a typed, versioned agent-policy registry (allowed autonomy modes, browser/connector/MCP enablement, egress tier, memory, scheduled agents) with per-key fail-closed values and lock states shown in chat/agent settings.
verevon.strengths: Capability rollout and scope grants already give admins per-capability control.

clusters.benefit: Enterprise buyers expect to cap what agents can do; a fail-closed registry prevents silent widening when config breaks.
clusters.approach: Control Plane owns the registry schema (Rust/Go shared JSON schema); Model Plane reads a signed org policy snapshot at run start (like Space decisions) and clamps; SPA settings render lock states from the same schema.
clusters.risks: Schema sprawl; start with 10-15 keys.
clusters.rationale: Table-stakes for enterprise; Verevon has pieces but no registry.

clusters.name: Device-managed configuration delivery (GPO/MDM/bootstrap/helper)
clusters.description: Policies delivered through OS management (Windows GPO, macOS MDM, /etc files), bootstrap URLs and helper executables, with consent for code-executing keys.

bestInClass.why: Claude's layered tiers and per-user consent for code-executing delivered keys (q5).

clusters.mechanism: Read policy sources in priority order; validate; keys that execute code need user consent.

verevon.gap: Not applicable to a hosted web product; org policy is server-side.

clusters.approach: Skip; org policy lives in Control Plane.
clusters.rationale: Desktop deployment concern.

clusters.name: Tool-call policy as code (CEL rules, external decision endpoint)
clusters.description: Admins govern every tool call with expression rules (allow/deny/require_approval) or delegate to an HTTPS policy decision endpoint that fails closed.

bestInClass.why: Claude only (SRC, unreleased): up to 100 CEL rules where any deny wins, and an endpoint with onFailure=deny and a timeout.

clusters.mechanism: Rules {id, condition CEL over (tool, args, session, user), action, reason}; evaluate all, any deny wins; or POST the call to an endpoint with a 1-10 s timeout and onFailure deny.

verevon.gap: No baseline record in this category; the baseline narrative shows every dispatch calls capability-core EvaluatePolicy (a central decision point; Allow needs Ed25519-signed evidence; unknown tools fail closed). Missing: admin-authored expression rules over arguments. Capability-before-dispatch with health attestation is partial: 9 capabilities sit in an unattested quarantine baseline and every promotion-ledger row is source_only (v-planned-decisions-138).
verevon.strengths: Verevon already has the external-PDP architecture Claude is only now adding.

clusters.benefit: Lets enterprises encode their own rules without Verevon code changes.
clusters.approach: capability-core: optional CEL (cel-go) rules per org evaluated inside EvaluatePolicy; reasons surfaced on denials.
clusters.risks: Rule errors locking users out; validate and dry-run.
clusters.rationale: Verevon's PDP is a strength; CEL is an add-on.

clusters.name: Per-connector and per-tool permission policies (allow / ask / block)
clusters.description: Users and admins set each connector tool to always allow, needs approval or blocked, with graduated read / low-risk / all tiers and write tools defaulting to ask.

bestInClass.why: ChatGPT's graduated app permissions (Always ask / read / low-risk / all, per connected account) are the clearest UX (DOC q5); Claude's code (SRC q5) defaults all write tools of built-in connectors to ask and pins 8 high-impact tools per connector that can never be set to allow.

clusters.mechanism: Policy per (org, user, connector, tool) with tiers derived from declared side effects; default ask for writes; a never-allow set per connector that wildcards cannot open; server-side enforcement on each call; team defaults with batch update.

verevon.gap: Provider actions are a curated catalogue with capability policy and scopes, and only 8 registry actions are model-executable with written evidence. Missing: a user/admin-facing per-connector, per-tool allow/ask/block setting with graduated tiers; MCP tools are blocked entirely.
verevon.strengths: Evidence bar for model-executable actions is stricter than any reference.

clusters.benefit: Connectors (Gmail, Slack, GitHub, Microsoft) are core to Do mode; per-tool control lets users enable them confidently.
clusters.approach: capability-core: connector_tool_policy table (org default, user override, never_allow set from the catalogue); execution-core reads it in EvaluatePolicy; SPA connector settings page with tier selector.
clusters.risks: Users choosing 'allow all'; keep never-allow tools.
clusters.rationale: Prevalent and directly user-visible; Verevon's connectors need it to scale.

clusters.name: Connector write-path safeguards and scope-aware tool exposure
clusters.description: Safeguards inside connectors: rate limits and recipient caps on sends, allowlisted HTML, AI-generated headers, content-free audit, tools exposed only when the OAuth scope was granted, natural-language action constraints, account/org binding, shared vs personal connections.

bestInClass.why: Claude's Microsoft 365 server (q5 SRC) throttles writes (10/60 s), sends (5/5 min) and recipients (100/5 min) per user hash, sanitises HTML, stamps an AI-generated header, logs without content and registers tools only for granted Entra scopes; ChatGPT turns builder-written NL constraints into reviewable rules; Codex separates shared and personal connections for agents.

clusters.mechanism: Per-user sliding-window buckets keyed by a hashed principal; recipient units charged per send; tools filtered by granted scopes at registration; denials name the missing permission; audit events carry ids and counts, never content.

verevon.gap: No baseline record in this category. Deterministic postcondition read-backs verify provider writes. Not found: per-user send/recipient throttles, scope-aware tool exposure, AI-generated markers on outbound content, NL action constraints, shared vs personal connection model for deployed agents (verify in integration-corev2).
verevon.strengths: Postcondition verification of effects is ahead of all references.

clusters.benefit: Bounds damage from a hijacked agent and helps compliance (EU AI Act labelling of AI-generated content).
clusters.approach: integration-corev2: per-principal write/recipient buckets and scope-filtered action lists; Model Plane surfaces 'missing permission' typed errors; add an AI-generated header option on mail actions.
clusters.risks: Throttles frustrating bulk use cases; make them org-configurable.
clusters.rationale: Common pattern; Verevon partly ahead on verification.

clusters.name: MCP transport-level gate, consent receipts and server hygiene
clusters.description: One choke point for every MCP tool call with a decision cascade, single-use consent receipts bound to a hash of the exact arguments, reserved internal server names, manifest-pinned prompts, URL-elicitation guards and admin-gated inbound channels.

bestInClass.why: Only Claude (q5 SRC): the gate validates frames, lists tools itself and refuses ambiguous names; the permission layer mints a 120 s single-use receipt keyed by session, tool and SHA-256 of the arguments that the gate spends.

clusters.mechanism: Wrap MCP transport; reject malformed frames and unlisted tools; on approval mint receipt(session, tool, sha256(canonical args)); the gate executes only on spending a live matching receipt; drop servers whose names collide with reserved prefixes.

verevon.gap: MCP tools cannot be invoked by either loop until capability-core provides a durable binding (deliberate). When MCP is enabled, none of this gating exists yet.
verevon.strengths: Blocking MCP until effects are verifiable is the safe choice.

clusters.benefit: MCP is how users bring their own tools; Claude's receipt pattern maps directly onto Verevon's exact-effect descriptors.
clusters.approach: capability-core MCP binding issues per-tool capability ids; execution-core gate with argument-hash receipts reusing approval descriptors; reserved server name prefixes in capability-core.
clusters.risks: MCP servers returning injected content; combine with C-t3-11-022.
clusters.rationale: Needed before MCP ships; single source.

clusters.name: Extension, plugin and skill supply-chain security
clusters.description: Install pipeline for skills/plugins/extensions: private copy, signature verification, org allowlist and security blocklist, trust-tiered static scanning with an un-overridable dangerous verdict, hook trust by hash, and scan-before-activate.

bestInClass.why: Claude's hardened install (signature, identity binding, blocklist hash) and server-side scan gate where the previous version stays live until the scan passes (q5); Hermes's trust-tier x verdict matrix; Codex's trusted-hash approval for project and plugin hooks.

clusters.mechanism: Upload -> copy to private storage -> verify signature/manifest -> hash checked against org allowlist and global blocklist -> static scan (patterns + AST) -> policy matrix (trust tier x verdict) -> activate; previous version serves until pass; hooks run only when their content hash is approved.

verevon.gap: No plugin or extension marketplace; skills exist (reattach_skill, skill injection switch) but no install scanning was checked.

clusters.benefit: Needed before user- or org-authored skills/plugins are shared (Codex-style plugin system is in the vision).
clusters.approach: Model Plane skill registry: scan on upload (pattern + LLM review), version pinning, org allowlist, publisher signatures later.
clusters.risks: Scanners give false confidence; state the trust model.
clusters.rationale: Depends on a plugin system that does not exist yet.

clusters.name: Hooks as the policy enforcement point (PreToolUse chain)
clusters.description: A registered chain of pre-tool hooks enforces workspace fences, write guards and canonicalisation for every tool call, in addition to the approval prompt.

bestInClass.why: Claude (SRC): the desktop registers a PreToolUse chain (folder deny, worktree guard, config-root fence, cross-session send guard).

clusters.mechanism: Ordered hooks with matchers; each returns allow/deny/ask with a reason; run before permission resolution.

verevon.gap: No baseline record in this category; the baseline narrative shows a real hook engine (allow/deny/ask, globs) whose rules live in an in-memory gateway registry and are passed only on browser runs; the Do-mode loop passes an empty hook_context.
verevon.strengths: Hook engine exists in the governed pipeline.

clusters.benefit: Org policy hooks would apply uniformly to Do runs once wired.
clusters.approach: Persist hook rules in capability-core (not process memory); pass them into Do-mode hook_context; expose admin-defined hooks via the policy registry.
clusters.rationale: Small wiring fix with policy payoff.

clusters.name: Privacy modes and training/data-use controls
clusters.description: User/org privacy levels that decide what may be stored, logged or used for training, by data classification and purpose, signalled on every request and attested by the server.

bestInClass.why: Cursor's purpose-by-classification matrix (q5 SRC) with a privacy header on every request and server attestation of privacy pods; ChatGPT's training defaults for business tiers and consumer opt-out.

clusters.mechanism: Mode enum; policy(mode, field_class, purpose) -> allow|deny; request header carries mode; server confirms it runs a privacy-mode pod; features that need more data are withheld.

verevon.gap: Privacy tiers route to providers by residency/contract and ZDR is a non-downgradable claim. Missing: a user-visible statement per provider of training/use posture and a field-classification x purpose matrix for logging (verify Control Plane settings).
verevon.strengths: ZDR claim that requests cannot downgrade and privacy-tier routing are stronger than Cursor's header.

clusters.benefit: Clear 'your data is never used for training' posture per provider increases B2B trust.
clusters.approach: Show provider data-use posture in the model picker (from capability-core provider metadata); keep ZDR as the strict mode.
clusters.rationale: Mostly a disclosure gap on top of strong mechanics.

clusters.name: Zero Data Retention and residency boundaries
clusters.description: Per-product or per-org ZDR with clear exclusions, residency for data and inference, and admin notice of what ZDR disables.

bestInClass.why: Claude's per-product ZDR toggle with propagation notice (SRC); ChatGPT and Claude.ai document exactly which features ZDR excludes (DOC).

clusters.mechanism: Org/product flag; a feature matrix states what is disabled under ZDR; residency per tenant; admin UI notice that changes take minutes.

verevon.gap: Design is ahead of every reference (one resolver, signed non-downgradable claim, evidence-bound provider attestation, typed localised refusals, one-way org raise at the BFF), but no provider is attested, so every ZDR turn is refused and Temporary chat is unavailable in practice; the own-connection waiver is planned (Z-15 held); the org ZDR switch awaits a live proof.
verevon.strengths: Best-in-category design: fail-closed propagation across planes, typed refusals, retention receipts.

clusters.benefit: Unblocking one attested provider turns a paper strength into a shipped differentiator (Temporary chat, ZDR orgs).
clusters.approach: Operator step: attest one provider (contract evidence + review-by date) in inference-core; run the live proof for the org switch; then ship Temporary chat. Keep the waiver held until reviewed.
clusters.risks: Attesting without real contractual ZDR would be a compliance failure.
clusters.rationale: Verevon's strongest governance asset is currently unusable; small effort to unlock.

clusters.name: Retention periods, legal hold, deletion and temporary chats
clusters.description: Admin-set retention per product, suspension of deletion for legal hold, self-serve deletion, incognito/temporary chats and regulatory deletion tooling.

bestInClass.why: Claude implements policy-driven retention per surface with legal hold and a headless sweep (SRC); ChatGPT and Perplexity document concrete windows and incognito behaviour.

clusters.mechanism: Retention policy per org and surface; sweep job deletes inactive sessions past the window unless on hold; deletions propagate to search indexes and derived memory; temporary chats skip persistence.

verevon.gap: GDPR org/user erasure and Space deletion reconciliation are shipped; Temporary chat is built but gated off by the missing ZDR attestation. Not found: org-configurable retention windows and legal hold for threads/runs (verify session-core).
verevon.strengths: Erasure consumers with semantic-memory receipts are solid.

clusters.benefit: Enterprises require retention windows and legal hold before deploying chat broadly.
clusters.approach: session-core retention sweeper driven by a Control Plane retention policy (per org, per surface) with a hold flag; propagate deletes to Data Plane indexes and memory.
clusters.risks: Accidental mass deletion; dry-run and audit.
clusters.rationale: Common enterprise requirement.

clusters.name: Telemetry privacy and data-flow disclosures
clusters.description: Telemetry scrubbed through closed vocabularies, consent-separated collection and sending, typed event schemas as the privacy boundary, and consent points that state what data goes where.

bestInClass.why: Claude's scrub framework (q5) hashes third-party tool names, redacts keys/URLs and bounds free text per sink; DeepSeek declares every analytics event at compile time; Hermes separates collect and send consents. Counter-examples: DeepSeek default-on session-log upload and T3 Code hashed provider identity.

clusters.mechanism: Typed event enum with allowed attributes only; a scrubber per sink; opt-in/opt-out switches with disclosed consequences; consent dialogs list the data flow.

verevon.gap: Security events carry hashes only (shipped). Product analytics and frontend telemetry were not audited; check the SPA and gateway for analytics events and consent switches.
verevon.strengths: Hash-only security events.

clusters.benefit: Consistent with ZDR promises; avoids leaking prompts through observability.
clusters.approach: Typed event registry shared by the SPA and services; scrub at the OTel exporter; Control Plane privacy settings.
clusters.rationale: Hygiene; not user-visible.

clusters.name: Audit logs, compliance API and SIEM export
clusters.description: Append-only audit of agent actions, approvals, connector calls and admin changes, exposed through a compliance API and real-time export to SIEM.

bestInClass.why: ChatGPT's immutable Compliance Logs Platform plus stateful API with per-category admin keys (DOC); Perplexity streams audit JSON (queries, answers with model/sources, agent actions) by webhook to Splunk/Slack (DOC); Cursor records tool, hook, sandbox and classifier events (SRC). DeepSeek records approvals without actor identity (gap example).

clusters.mechanism: Transactional outbox per service -> audit core (append-only, hash-chained) -> query API with scoped admin keys + webhook/SIEM fan-out; each approval event carries actor, decision, scope and evidence ids.

verevon.gap: No baseline record in this category; the baseline narrative shows the session-core audit outbox to Audit Core was never delivered (4,992 events), with a fix built but not deployed; the capability registry has its own audit log. No compliance API or SIEM export found.
verevon.strengths: Transactional outbox design and a candid postmortem.

clusters.benefit: Enterprise and regulated customers require an audit trail of AI actions; it also backs ZDR and approval claims.
clusters.approach: Deploy the outbox fix; Control Plane Audit Core exposes a compliance query API and webhook export; include approval actor/scope and run proof-bundle ids.
clusters.risks: Audit logs must themselves respect ZDR (ids and hashes only).
clusters.rationale: Built but undelivered; enterprise blocker.

clusters.name: Identity, RBAC, SSO/SCIM and spend limits
clusters.description: Enterprise identity and access: SSO, SCIM, custom roles and groups, domain verification, IP allowlists, per-group/per-member credit caps.

bestInClass.why: ChatGPT's additive RBAC with custom roles, groups and delegated managers (DOC) is the most complete; Claude.ai and Perplexity add group spend limits and IP allowlisting.

clusters.mechanism: Roles with permission sets combined additively; SCIM group sync maps to roles; spend caps per group/member enforced at the gateway.

verevon.gap: Shipped in Control Plane (members, SSO, org security, quotas) with Model Plane rate limits, org quota and budget checks. Weaknesses: the org quota fails open on an org-core outage and has no reservation; per-member credit caps not verified.
verevon.strengths: Org quota from Control plus cost-core budget checks and run budgets.

clusters.approach: Keep; consider fail-closed (or bounded) quota on org-core outage and per-member caps.
clusters.rationale: Verevon at parity.

clusters.name: Step-up verification and consumer account safety
clusters.description: Fresh passkey/security-key proof before sensitive approvals; passkey-only sign-in, parental controls, age prediction, trusted contacts.

bestInClass.why: Codex requires a fresh passkey proof for some approvals (SRC); ChatGPT documents consumer account safety (DOC).

clusters.mechanism: WebAuthn assertion bound to the approval id before high-risk effects execute.

verevon.gap: No baseline record. Check Control Plane for WebAuthn/passkeys and whether any approval can require step-up.

clusters.benefit: A strong pairing for payments, external sends and full-access escalation.
clusters.approach: Control Plane WebAuthn step-up endpoint returning a signed assertion that execution-core verifies before executing NeverAuto effects.
clusters.risks: Friction.
clusters.rationale: Only 2 sources; valuable later with payments.

clusters.name: Compliance-regime gating (HIPAA verdicts, org capability taints, placement rules)
clusters.description: Org capability tags (e.g. hipaa_regulated) latch restricted verdicts that disable whole surfaces, plus rules for where each surface may run and which inference providers are allowed.

bestInClass.why: Only Claude (SRC): a sticky HIPAA verdict blocks sharing, cloud hand-off and scheduled cloud tasks with one error type.

clusters.mechanism: Org taints from the server -> sticky restricted verdict -> a gate function throws a typed error for listed surfaces.

verevon.gap: Verevon has the same pattern for ZDR (a persistence-free path that disables memory, artifacts, Do mode and approvals) and sovereign/privacy-tier routing, but no general regime tags beyond ZDR and residency.
verevon.strengths: ZDR feature matrix is an equivalent, fail-closed design.

clusters.benefit: Generalising to regime tags (health, public sector) would be straightforward later.
clusters.approach: Add regime tags to the Control-signed org posture; reuse the zdr_features gate pattern.
clusters.rationale: Single source; Verevon has the pattern.

clusters.name: Sharing governance
clusters.description: Org-only sharing by default, admin control of external sharing and invites, revocation. (Supported only by DOC/INF records.)

bestInClass.why: Only source (DOC).

clusters.mechanism: Share links scoped to the org by default; admin toggles external sharing; revoke all.

verevon.gap: Shareable links are not built; Space access must never widen an owner-plane ACL. Related: support and foreign-origin threads are already rendered read-only (v-chat-agents-ui-136).

clusters.benefit: Required when share links ship.
clusters.approach: Design share links in session-core with org-only default, admin policy key and ZDR refusal.
clusters.rationale: Depends on a feature that does not exist.

clusters.name: Sandboxed rendering of generated content (artifacts, widgets, previews)
clusters.description: Model-generated HTML and app widgets render in isolated frames/sessions with deny-all permissions, request allowlists and controlled bridges to tools.

bestInClass.why: Claude's artifact renderer (deny-all session, request allowlist, TOCTOU-safe file serving) and artifact-to-connector bridge (declared tool allowlist, destructive confirmation, rate limit) are q5; Codex's MCP App sandbox host logs blocked navigation.

clusters.mechanism: Render in an opaque-origin iframe (sandbox allow-scripts, no same-origin) with CSP; any tool call from the artifact goes over postMessage to the host, checked against the artifact's declared allowlist and policy, with a card for destructive tools.

verevon.gap: HTML artifacts render in a srcdoc iframe with allow-scripts and no same-origin. There is no artifact-to-tool bridge (so no bridge policy is needed yet).
verevon.strengths: Correct opaque-origin isolation.

clusters.approach: Keep; if interactive artifacts that call tools are added, adopt Claude's declared-allowlist bridge.
clusters.rationale: At parity for what exists.

clusters.name: Client shell hardening and link/protocol safety
clusters.description: Desktop/web client hardening: sandboxed windows, sender-validated IPC, navigation and popup guards, deep-link validation, loopback host trust fences, confirmations for external links and protocols, deceptive-link warnings.

bestInClass.why: Claude covers the most ground (typed IPC with sender validation, navigation guards, link confirmations with 'user@host' deception warnings); most items are Electron-specific.

clusters.mechanism: For a web SPA: CSP, rel=noopener, an interstitial for external links from model output, warnings for deceptive URLs, no javascript: or custom protocols.

verevon.gap: No baseline record. Check the SPA markdown renderer for external-link interstitials and protocol filtering. Desktop items do not apply.

clusters.benefit: Model output links are an injection/phishing vector.
clusters.approach: SPA: link interstitial for model-generated links to new domains; block non-http(s) schemes; CSP review.
clusters.rationale: Mostly desktop-specific.

clusters.name: Service authentication, RPC scope tables and tenancy chokepoints
clusters.description: Every RPC requires a declared scope and authenticated tenant; per-audience delegated tokens; single-use WebSocket tickets; external surfaces refuse work until authorised.

bestInClass.why: T3 Code's total RPC scope map where a missing scope is a compile error (q5) is the cleanest; Hermes adds single-use 30 s WebSocket tickets and the rule that session ids are not authorisation.

clusters.mechanism: A total map method -> required scope checked in one interceptor; tokens per audience; WS upgrade via short-lived single-use ticket.

verevon.gap: Fail-closed RS256/JWKS on every service, authorize_rpc over every RPC and per-audience delegated bearers from the BFF are shipped. Remaining: verified tenant delegation for background workers (per-principal allowlists only) and NATS without TLS/mTLS/workload identity.
verevon.strengths: Ahead of every reference on service-to-service authority and tenancy.

clusters.approach: Keep; close NATS mTLS and verified worker delegation.
clusters.risks: Plaintext NATS inside the cluster is the weakest link.
clusters.rationale: Verevon's strongest area besides ZDR.

clusters.name: Device pairing and remote-control trust
clusters.description: Pairing codes/QR for clients, device-bound login and revocation, hardware attestation of remote sessions, SSH host-key-first prompts, consent before exposing local folders remotely, messaging-gateway DM pairing.

bestInClass.why: Claude's device-key signing of session binds and triggers (q5); T3 Code's pairing with device list and revoke; Hermes's DM pairing codes with lockout.

clusters.mechanism: One-time pairing code -> scoped session per device; device list with revoke; hardware-backed key signs sensitive binds.

verevon.gap: Not applicable to a browser-first hosted product; messaging-channel pairing belongs to the docs-only Channel Plane.

clusters.benefit: Relevant only for a future Channel Plane (Telegram/Slack bots).
clusters.approach: Skip now; reuse Hermes's pairing pattern when Channel Plane starts.
clusters.rationale: Local/desktop concern; Channel Plane is future.

clusters.name: Release, update and dependency supply-chain integrity
clusters.description: Signed releases and updaters, hash-checked installers, upper-bounded and SHA-pinned dependencies and actions, release-age checks, server-driven mandatory updates.

bestInClass.why: Hermes (q5 SRC): every dependency upper-bounded, git URLs and Actions pinned to SHAs, a release-age check. Counter-examples: Antigravity and Manus ship unsigned Windows binaries.

clusters.mechanism: Lockfiles with exact pins; CI actions by SHA; minimum release age before adoption; signed artifacts with rollback.

verevon.gap: Artifact v3 tooling exists but no signed candidate or rollback artifact has been built; dependency pinning policy not audited.

clusters.benefit: A signed, reproducible release is a prerequisite for credible security claims to enterprise buyers.
clusters.approach: Build and sign the release artifact in CI; pin GitHub Actions by SHA; add cargo-deny/govulncheck gates.
clusters.rationale: Built tooling, not used.
